title: Composing three in a row
idea: Composing functions: chain three sub-plans, resolving inside-out. Longer chains are just the same rule applied again.

exercises.prompt:
Read:

def double(n):
    return n * 2

def add_one(n):
    return n + 1

print(double(add_one(double(3))))

Which runs FIRST?
exercises.explanation: Always the innermost first: double(3) -> 6. Then work outward.

exercises.prompt: Trace double(add_one(double(3))) step by step. Put the steps in order.
exercises.explanation: Inner double(3)=6, then add_one(6)=7, then outer double(7)=14. Inside-out, three times.
double(3)=6, add_one(6)=7, double(7)=14. The final value is 14.

exercises.prompt: A longer chain uses the SAME inside-out rule — just applied more times.
exercises.explanation: Yes. Two calls or five, you resolve the innermost first each time. No new rule, just more steps.

exercises.prompt:
Trace:

def triple(n):
    return n * 3

print(triple(triple(triple(1))))
exercises.explanation: triple(1)=3, triple(3)=9, triple(9)=27. Each layer multiplies by 3, inside-out.
add_one(2) is 3. Replace it, then continue: double(3)=6, add_one(6)=7.

exercises.prompt: Why keep each sub-plan small even when chaining several?
options: Small pieces are easy to reuse and combine in different orders
exercises.explanation: Small, single-job sub-plans snap together in many ways. That's the power of composing.

exercises.prompt: REVIEW: a long chain can also be written with middle variables. That is...
options: allowed and often clearer than deep nesting
exercises.explanation: Deep nesting can get hard to read. Named middle steps show each stage — same result, clearer.

options: Chaining three (or more) sub-plans uses the same inside-out rule
long chains need a new rule
order doesn't matter in long chains
exercises.explanation: Resolve innermost first, repeat outward. The rule scales to any number of composed calls.
